t: #2202 Maximize the Topmost Element After K Moves
o: Each move pops the top or pushes back a previously popped element. After exactly k moves the pile must be non-empty (otherwise return -1). In Example 1, popping three elements and restoring 5 yields top 5. In Example 2, a single-element pile with k=1 forces a pop leaving an empty pile, hence -1. Key observations: with k moves you can expose any of the first k-1 elements (pop them away and restore the best), or if k < n you can simply pop exactly k times landing on nums[k-1].
k: With k moves you can bring any of nums[0..k-2] to the top: pop everything above it and restore it.
If k < n, popping exactly k times leaves nums[k-1] on top — another candidate.
k = 1 always returns -1 (forced pop); if k > n the pile empties, but spare moves let you finish with any element, so the answer is max(nums).

a.i: Enumerate the reachable tops directly: the best of the first k-1 elements, nums[k-1] when k < n, and max(nums) when k > n. Handle k = 0 (answer nums[0]) and k = 1 (-1) specially.
s: If k == 0 return nums[0]; if k == 1 return -1.
If k < n, candidate nums[k-1]; if k > n, candidate max(nums).
a.t: O(min(k, n)) — one scan of the relevant prefix (and possibly the whole array).

a.i: Precompute prefMax[i] = max(nums[0..i]) so each reachability case becomes an O(1) lookup. This cleanly separates the logic and generalizes if reachability rules change.
s: Build prefMax where prefMax[i] = max(prefMax[i-1], nums[i]).
Apply the same case analysis using prefMax lookups.
a.t: O(n) — building the prefix max dominates.

w: The tricky parts are the boundary cases: k=0, k=1, k=n (popping everything leaves nothing to land on, so nums[n-1] is NOT reachable via pure pops), and k>n. Test each explicitly. A common bug is treating k==n like k<n. Follow-up: what if pushes could add arbitrary values? Then the answer changes completely.
